ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> We recruited 120 English-speaking young adults through the psychology research participant pool at Boston University and through study advertisements posted in the Greater Boston metropolitan area between September 2021 and December 2022.

> Participants completed a baseline assessment followed by a 14-day EMA period and provided written informed consent prior to participation.

> Participants recruited through the university pool received up to four course credits; community participants received up to a $60 gift card.

> Nearly all participants were undergraduate or graduate students (93.24%).

> The 74 participants completed 2,773 prompts (M = 37.47 of 56), and 515 (18.6%) had no GPS fix within 15 minutes and were excluded, leaving 2,258 prompts for the athome models.

> In addition, because Jasmine does not readily generate a binary indicator of whether participants were at home at the exact time of each EMA prompt, we implemented a data-driven clustering approach to estimate participants' home locations from raw, unprocessed GPS data.

> Excluded participants provided EMA data but lacked usable GPS data, a detectable home location, or hourly passive-sensing output (see Participants).

> Panel (A) displays the proportion of EMA prompts at which participants were classified as being at home versus outside the home across the four daily time blocks (morning: 8-11:59 AM; midday: 12-3:59 PM; afternoon: 4-7:59 PM; evening: 8-11 PM).

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethical approval was granted by the Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Review Board (Protocol #5684E).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Digital Phenotyping of Isolation and Loneliness (DPhIL)
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
Research Question 1: Can we reliably classify social isolation and loneliness through integration of active (EMA) and passive (movement, location, conversation, and phone use) smartphone data? (Phase I)
Research Question 2: Can we use integrated active and passive smartphone data to predict within-person transitions across momentary states of social isolation and loneliness? (Phase I)
Research Question 3: To what extent will these predictions fit a clinical sample characterized by social isolation and loneliness? (Phase II)
table.design_dependent_variables:
Momentary loneliness: 3-item (Hughes et al., 2004; used in Phase I) and 4-item (Russell et al., 1980; used in Phase II) UCLA Loneliness Scales.
Momentary Social Isolation: Single item question regarding presence and degree of social interaction.
All momentary measures assessed via EMA self-report using a smartphone data collection app, 4 times per day for 14 days.
table.statistical_tests:
Research Question 1: We will use a mixed effects (multilevel) modeling approach to understand the within-person (Level 1; e.g., EMA reports of affect, interaction quality) and between-person (Level 2; e.g., baseline assessments of social connection, mood/anxiety symptoms, etc.) predictors of momentary reports of social isolation and loneliness. Level 1 predictors identified in these models will inform the classification of within-person momentary social activity states (isolation and loneliness), while Level 2 predictors will add precision to these classifications through identification of important moderators. Variables identified in these models will form the basis for network analyses conducted in Research Question 2.
Research Question 2: In the first approach, we will detect change points in dynamic correlation networks from temporally-dense data. We will observe a series of active and passive smartphone data streams that will be represented by network nodes. We will compute their correlations over a period of time (e.g., every few hours) to create a correlation matrix of these nodes. We will start with the assumption that there will be several correlation matrices, within and between people, that will roughly correspond to our postulated states of social isolation and loneliness. For every time window, we estimate which correlation matrix (state) most likely gave rise to the observed data. We will rely on indicators identified in prior analyses to label various states of social isolation and loneliness. These states will include the various social isolation classifications that vary within people. In our second approach, we will implement Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to examine the distributional properties of variables for state space transition. Here we will use the hidden state to model underlying factors that cannot be directly observed and the observed state to model the transitions across states. We anticipate the need to implement an Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approach to handle some cases.
Research Question 3: The analytic plan will follow the same basic structure as in Q2. We will also test competing models for changes in fit using common fit indices (e.g., AIC/BIC, log likelihood). Primary model comparison will include testing the difference between models of objective social isolation in the clinical and healthy samples, and between models of loneliness in the samples. We will then test iterative model fit analyses to identify key within- and between-person predictors of social activity state transitions.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: We will only exclude observations that fall outside plausible response options for both baseline surveys and momentary/ambulatory data. For baseline surveys, this could include responses with little to no variability (e.g., all options either 'none' or 'extremely') or substantial missingness (e.g., only 1-2 valid responses on a longer questionnaire). For EMA data, we will exclude responses that are completed too quickly (e.g., under 2 sec per question). We will also exclude EMA data where there are fewer than 25% of possible responses completed (i.e., < 14 out of 56 possible surveys).
table.sample_size:
Phase I: 100 adults without serious mental illness. Determined based on power to identify group-level predictors of momentary isolation and loneliness with moderate effect sizes, and to detect within-person transition states of isolation and loneliness with moderate probability.
Phase II: 50 adults with serious mental illness. Determined based on power to detect within-person transition states.
table.additional_comments:
All methodological and analytic details provided above were transferred directly from a NIH grant proposal ("Passive Sensing of Social Isolation: A Digital Phenotyping Approach," R01MH122367). Thus, while data collection is currently ongoing, analytic decisions were prior to data collection.

Additional measures collected: Baseline assessments include gold standard assessments of social functioning, including Heinrich's Quality of Life – Interpersonal Relations scale (QLS-IR) and the Social Functioning Scale (SFS). We also administer the 20-item UCLA Loneliness Scale to assess dispositional loneliness and self-report forms of social support and connection (Social Provisions Scale; SPS). EMA surveys include questions assessing 1) presence and number of recent interactions ("How many interactions have you had in the past three hours?"), 2) quality of interactions ("How did those interactions go?", "How do you feel you came across to others in those interactions?"), and 3) perceptions of connection and loneliness ("How lonely do you feel right now?". Passive sensor data will include raw ambient audio data collected via smartphone microphone, call and text log data, and mobility data via smartphone GPS. For Phase II: we will also assess psychiatric symptoms and other clinical measures relevant for social connection.

table.header: Conclusions
Conclusions
Conclusions

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 231 columns across 30 data files.
#### Issues Identified

83 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We recruited 120 English-speaking young adults through the psychology research participant pool at Boston University and through study advertisements posted in the Greater Boston metropolitan area between September 2021 and December 2022.
Participants completed a baseline assessment followed by a 14-day EMA period and provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Participants recruited through the university pool received up to four course credits; community participants received up to a $60 gift card.
Nearly all participants were undergraduate or graduate students (93.24%).
The 74 participants completed 2,773 prompts (M = 37.47 of 56), and 515 (18.6%) had no GPS fix within 15 minutes and were excluded, leaving 2,258 prompts for the athome models.

In addition, because Jasmine does not readily generate a binary indicator of whether participants were at home at the exact time of each EMA prompt, we implemented a data-driven clustering approach to estimate participants' home locations from raw, unprocessed GPS data.
Excluded participants provided EMA data but lacked usable GPS data, a detectable home location, or hourly passive-sensing output (see Participants).

Panel (A) displays the proportion of EMA prompts at which participants were classified as being at home versus outside the home across the four daily time blocks (morning: 8-11:59 AM; midday: 12-3:59 PM; afternoon: 4-7:59 PM; evening: 8-11 PM).

text.text: Momentary emotional experience is shaped by the contexts in which individuals are embedded, yet little is known about how time spent in certain locations (e.g., at home versus in public spaces) relates to affect in daily life.
In the current study, 74 young adults completed 14 days of smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment and GPS-based geolocation.

We examined three contextual dimensions in relation to momentary affect (happiness, anxiety, and sadness) in young adults: environmental context (at home versus outside), recent exposure duration (time spent at home in the preceding three hours), and temporal context (time of day and day of week).
Multilevel models indicated that participants reported higher happiness and lower anxiety in the evening relative to morning, and higher happiness on weekends than on weekdays.
Within individuals, being at home (and time spent at home) was associated with lower happiness than being outside the home.
Furthermore, the exploratory analysis suggested that the association between time spent at home and lower happiness was stronger among individuals who typically spent less time at home.
These findings suggest that temporal and environmental contexts are associated with momentary happiness, whereas environmental context was not associated with anxiety or sadness.
Affect fluctuates dynamically in daily life (Koval et al., 2013; Kuppens et al., 2010; Li et al., 2026) and plays a central role in psychological well-being (Posner et al., 2005; Trull et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Affect fluctuates dynamically in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Koval et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kuppens et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2026)</ref> and plays a central role in psychological well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Posner et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Trull et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These fluctuations are shaped by the contexts in which individuals are embedded, including where they spend their time and for how long, and when within daily and weekly rhythms those exposures occur.

Young adulthood is characterized by elevated loneliness and a particularly vulnerable developmental window for the onset of psychological disorders (Li et al., 2025; Pedrelli et al., 2015; Shah & Househ, 2023; Storrie et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Young adulthood is characterized by elevated loneliness and a particularly vulnerable developmental window for the onset of psychological disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Li et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Pedrelli et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Shah & Househ, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Storrie et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This period involves significant life transitions, including changes in social networks, academic pressures, and evolving autonomy (Kohler Giancola et al., 2009; Saleh et al., 2017); these circumstances may amplify the influence of daily contexts, such as social engagement, isolation, and activity patterns, on emotional well-being.
text.formatted: This period involves significant life transitions, including changes in social networks, academic pressures, and evolving autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kohler Giancola et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Saleh et al., 2017)</ref>; these circumstances may amplify the influence of daily contexts, such as social engagement, isolation, and activity patterns, on emotional well-being.

text.text: Examining how environmental context shapes momentary affect during this life stage may therefore provide insight into how daily contexts influence emotional experiences.
Recent advances in digital assessment methods have expanded researchers' ability to study psychological processes in naturalistic settings.

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) allows for repeated, real-time measurement of individuals' affect, behavior, and context, providing insights into within-person dynamics as they unfold in daily life (Shiffman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) allows for repeated, real-time measurement of individuals' affect, behavior, and context, providing insights into within-person dynamics as they unfold in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Shiffman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: EMA studies have demonstrated that emotions vary within individuals over time, reflecting both internal regulation processes and changing environmental contexts (Chen et al., 2024 (Chen et al., , 2026;; Ebner-Priemer & Trull, 2009; Trull et al., 2015).
text.formatted: EMA studies have demonstrated that emotions vary within individuals over time, reflecting both internal regulation processes and changing environmental contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ebner-Priemer & Trull, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Trull et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These within-person fluctuations are clinically meaningful; for example, intraindividual variability in negative affect is associated with future depressive symptoms (Wichers et al., 2010), as well as the onset of bipolar spectrum disorders over time (Sperry et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These within-person fluctuations are clinically meaningful; for example, intraindividual variability in negative affect is associated with future depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wichers et al., 2010)</ref>, as well as the onset of bipolar spectrum disorders over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Sperry et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Digital phenotyping leverages passive data collected from personal digital devices to capture indicators of movement, app usage, communication (text messages and calling), and geolocation, without requiring active participant input and thereby reducing participant burden (Langener et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2023; Torous et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Digital phenotyping leverages passive data collected from personal digital devices to capture indicators of movement, app usage, communication (text messages and calling), and geolocation, without requiring active participant input and thereby reducing participant burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Langener et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lee et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Torous et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When combined with EMA, passive sensing enables researchers to examine how contextual data correspond to individuals' momentary emotional experiences in real time, allowing fine-grained analyses of how daily environments shape affect as it unfolds (Fulford & Jacobson, 2025; Langener et al., 2024; Torous et al., 2016).
text.formatted: When combined with EMA, passive sensing enables researchers to examine how contextual data correspond to individuals' momentary emotional experiences in real time, allowing fine-grained analyses of how daily environments shape affect as it unfolds <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fulford & Jacobson, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Langener et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Torous et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Among passive sensing indicators, GPS-based geolocation data (e.g., time spent at home, distance traveled, and number of locations visited) have been widely used to examine associations between mobility and mental health outcomes (Auerbach et al., 2022; Barnett & Onnela, 2020; Filip et al., 2025; Fulford et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Among passive sensing indicators, GPS-based geolocation data (e.g., time spent at home, distance traveled, and number of locations visited) have been widely used to examine associations between mobility and mental health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Auerbach et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Barnett & Onnela, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Filip et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fulford et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, reduced mobilitycharacterized by shorter distances traveled, fewer locations visited, less variability in locations visited (i.e., entropy), and greater time spent at home-has been linked to greater depression symptoms, stress, and negative affect (Auerbach et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2024; Filip et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specifically, reduced mobilitycharacterized by shorter distances traveled, fewer locations visited, less variability in locations visited (i.e., entropy), and greater time spent at home-has been linked to greater depression symptoms, stress, and negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Auerbach et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Choi et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Filip et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, broader evidence suggests that spending more time at home is associated with greater negative symptom burden and functional impairment among individuals with serious mental illness (Filip et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, broader evidence suggests that spending more time at home is associated with greater negative symptom burden and functional impairment among individuals with serious mental illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Filip et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To date, digital phenotyping studies have typically examined geolocation data aggregated at the daily or weekly level, such as average time spent at home or total daily movement.

Although informative, these summary indicators may overlook potentially important temporal dynamics: short exposure windows may capture acute contextual influences on affect, whereas longer windows may reflect sustained behavioral patterns such as prolonged social engagement or withdrawal.
Additionally, little is known about how recent, short-term environmental exposure, measured over brief windows aligned with EMA prompts, relates to momentary affect.

For example, two days with the same total time at home or the same number of locations visited can still look very different hour by hour: on one day a participant may have just returned home before an afternoon prompt, whereas on another day the participant may have been at home for the entire afternoon.
Daily or weekly aggregates cannot distinguish these situations, yet they may correspond to distinct emotional experiences at the moment affect is assessed.
Evaluating affect across different timescales may therefore clarify how spatial context relates to dynamics of emotional experience.
The goal of the present study was to evaluate the impact of three related but conceptually distinct contexts on affect in daily life.
The environmental context is where an individual is located at a given moment.
In the present study, we operationalized environmental context as being at home versus outside the home.
Recent exposure duration is the time an individual spent in that environment.
In the present study, we operationalized this as the time spent at home (versus outside) within the 3-hour window preceding each EMA report, reflecting recent environmental exposure between prompts.
The temporal context is when that exposure occurs within broader daily rhythms, particularly the time of day (e.g., morning vs. evening) and the day of the week (e.g., weekday vs weekend).
Although these contextual factors are interrelated, each may influence emotional experience through distinct mechanisms.

Environmental context may influence emotional experience through two primary pathways: social (opportunities for interpersonal contact) and non-social (in out-of-home settings through drivers such as exposure to natural environments).
Time spent outside the home may increase opportunities for and variation in face-to-face interaction.

Extended time at home, for example, particularly when spent alone, may limit opportunities for social interaction, which has been associated with increased loneliness (Kuczynski et al., 2022; Sugiyama et al., 2008; Yanos et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Extended time at home, for example, particularly when spent alone, may limit opportunities for social interaction, which has been associated with increased loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kuczynski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Sugiyama et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yanos et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: For young adults whose social lives are often structured by work or school, prolonged residence at home could reflect social disengagement, potentially increasing risk for negative affect and associated mental health concerns.

In addition, exposure to varied environments outside the home, including natural settings such as parks and green spaces, has been associated with higher positive affect (Houlden et al., 2018; Kangarloo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In addition, exposure to varied environments outside the home, including natural settings such as parks and green spaces, has been associated with higher positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Houlden et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kangarloo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern is theoretically grounded in Attention Restoration Theory (R. Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989; S. Kaplan, 1995) and Stress Recovery Theory (Ulrich et al., 1991), both of which hold that natural and varied environments replenish attentional resources and reduce negative arousal, creating conditions more conducive to positive affect (Felsten, 2009; Houlden et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This pattern is theoretically grounded in Attention Restoration Theory (R. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989</ref>; S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kaplan, 1995)</ref> and Stress Recovery Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Ulrich et al., 1991)</ref>, both of which hold that natural and varied environments replenish attentional resources and reduce negative arousal, creating conditions more conducive to positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Felsten, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Houlden et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the home environment may reduce arousal and novelty-seeking, contributing to disengagement when exposure is prolonged.

For college students in particular, the home environment is often a functionally constrained space, frequently a dormitory room or shared apartment, with limited capacity for varied activities, making prolonged time at home especially likely to dampen positive affective states and potentially increase low-grade negative states such as boredom (Eastwood et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For college students in particular, the home environment is often a functionally constrained space, frequently a dormitory room or shared apartment, with limited capacity for varied activities, making prolonged time at home especially likely to dampen positive affective states and potentially increase low-grade negative states such as boredom <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eastwood et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Both the social and environmental pathways suggest that being at home, relative to being outside the home, may be associated with lower high-arousal positive affect and, with prolonged exposure, potentially higher negative states such as boredom.
It bears noting, however, that these expectations apply most clearly to high-arousal positive affect such as excitement or surprise (McManus et al., 2024; Russell, 1980; Swerdlow et al., 2022) 1 .
text.formatted: It bears noting, however, that these expectations apply most clearly to high-arousal positive affect such as excitement or surprise <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(McManus et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Russell, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Swerdlow et al., 2022)</ref> 1 .

text.text: Additionally, the emotional 1 In the present study, we operationalized positive affect using a single happiness item, which can be thought of as high arousal on the affective circumplex (Russell, 1980).
text.formatted: Additionally, the emotional 1 In the present study, we operationalized positive affect using a single happiness item, which can be thought of as high arousal on the affective circumplex <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Russell, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the experiences of a given environmental context may depend not only on where individuals are located but also on how long they have remained in that context.
Emotional experience is also shaped by temporal context, including both time of day and daily and weekly rhythms.
Research consistently demonstrates systematic diurnal patterns in affect.

In large population-based samples of adults, individuals tend to report the highest wellbeing and positive affect earlier in the day, with declines toward the evening, while negative affect and distress show corresponding increases, peaking later at night (Bu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In large population-based samples of adults, individuals tend to report the highest wellbeing and positive affect earlier in the day, with declines toward the evening, while negative affect and distress show corresponding increases, peaking later at night <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns likely reflect interactions among circadian processes, physiological rhythms, nutrition (e.g., caffeine or meal consumption), and the structured demands of daily activities such as work, study, and social engagement (Cardinali, 2000; Clark et al., 1989; Golder & Macy, 2011).
text.formatted: These patterns likely reflect interactions among circadian processes, physiological rhythms, nutrition (e.g., caffeine or meal consumption), and the structured demands of daily activities such as work, study, and social engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cardinali, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Clark et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Golder & Macy, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns may vary across populations, however; in young adults and college students, daytime hours structured around academic demands may shift peaks in positive affect toward the evening, when obligations recede and social opportunities increase.
Weekly rhythms also influence emotional experience.

Compared with weekdays, weekends are often associated with higher positive affect and lower negative affect, a pattern attributed to greater autonomy and increased opportunities for social interaction during non-obligatory days.

For young adults, this distinction may be particularly salient because weekdays are typically structured around work or academic responsibilities, whereas weekends allow greater flexibility in social and recreational activities (Adams et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For young adults, this distinction may be particularly salient because weekdays are typically structured around work or academic responsibilities, whereas weekends allow greater flexibility in social and recreational activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: predictions outlined here apply most directly to high-arousal positive affect states.
Being at home could also support low-arousal positive states, such as calmness or contentment.
Environmental and temporal contexts are closely intertwined in daily life.

Individuals differ in their daily routines, shaped by work schedules, lifestyles, and personal habits, yet a general pattern holds that people tend to spend more time at home during early-morning and latenight hours and more time outside during daytime hours.
Studies examining environmental context alone may therefore inadvertently confound location with time of day or week.
More importantly, time of day may moderate the psychological impact of variation in environmental context on affect.

For example, time spent at home on a weekday afternoon may reflect disengagement from academic or social activities, whereas the same amount of time at home on a weekend evening may reflect intentional leisure or rest.

From an appraisal perspective, the emotional significance of a situation depends on how it relates to an individual's goals and expectations, which themselves vary across daily rhythms (Ellsworth & Scherer, 2002; Li & Chen, 2026; Smith & Kirby, 2009).
text.formatted: From an appraisal perspective, the emotional significance of a situation depends on how it relates to an individual's goals and expectations, which themselves vary across daily rhythms <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Ellsworth & Scherer, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li & Chen, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Smith & Kirby, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Examining environmental exposure without considering time of day may therefore obscure meaningful heterogeneity in how contexts shape momentary emotional experiences.

By examining the current environmental context (at home versus outside the home), time spent in that environment over the past three hours, and variation across daily and weekly rhythms, we aimed to clarify how spatial and temporal contexts shape momentary emotional experience.

Our approach aligns geolocation-based indicators with the temporal scale at which momentary affect is assessed, allowing us to examine how short-term environmental exposure relates to emotional experience in daily life.
We also explored the extent to which time of day and day of the week moderated associations between spatial contexts and momentary affective outcomes.
Given the context-dependent nature of time spent at home, we did not impose directional hypotheses regarding moderation effects.
Data were collected as part of the Digital Phenotyping of Isolation and Loneliness (DPhIL) study (See more about the parent study at https://osf.io/42r3w).
text.formatted: Data were collected as part of the Digital Phenotyping of Isolation and Loneliness (DPhIL) study (See more about the parent study at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/42r3w">https://osf.io/42r3w</ref>).

text.text: We recruited 120 English-speaking young adults through the psychology research participant pool at Boston University and through study advertisements posted in the Greater Boston metropolitan area between September 2021 and December 2022.
Eligibility required owning a smartphone and willingness to install the study app.
Participants completed a baseline assessment followed by a 14-day EMA period and provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Among all participants, 113 completed the EMA phase or provided at least some EMA data.
Each EMA prompt was administered a minimum of 90 minutes apart throughout each day at pseudorandom time points within 8-11 AM, 12-3 PM, 4-7 PM, and 8-11 PM blocks.
Ethical approval was granted by the Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Review Board (Protocol #5684E).
Participants recruited through the university pool received up to four course credits; community participants received up to a $60 gift card.
Compensation was awarded proportionally to EMA adherence, with maximum compensation provided to participants who completed at least 75% (42) of 56 possible surveys.

Of the 113 participants who completed the EMA phase or provided at least some EMA data, 39 were excluded from analyses: seven had no GPS data collected during the study period, three had GPS data but insufficient nighttime observations to identify a stable home location cluster, three showed systematic home misclassification on GPS validation (100% false negative rate with ≥ 5 EMA-reported home observations), and 26 had GPS data too sparse to estimate hourly mobility, so the time-spent-at-home measure could not be computed for them.

These 26 participants did have a valid at-home classification, which is derived separately from raw GPS, and their agreement with self-reported location was comparable to that of the retained participants (86.5% with them included versus 86.7% without; see Passive Geolocation).
We nonetheless excluded them from all analyses so that every model was estimated on the same 74 participants, which allows the models with and without time spent at home to be compared directly.
The final sample therefore comprised 74 young adults (mean age = 21.68 years, SD = 6.32).
About half of the participants identified as female (54.05%).

The sample was racially and ethnically diverse: 47.30% Asian, 32.43% White, 5.41% Black, and 9.46% Multiracial; 10.81% of participants identified as Hispanic or Latine (reported as an overlapping ethnic category).
Nearly all participants were undergraduate or graduate students (93.24%).
See Table 1 for full demographic information.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table">1</ref> for full demographic information.

text.text: To assess the robustness of the final analytic sample, we compared the participants that were excluded based on GPS data quality on demographic characteristics (Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: To assess the robustness of the final analytic sample, we compared the participants that were excluded based on GPS data quality on demographic characteristics (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Excluded participants did not differ on gender, race, ethnicity, education level, or number of completed EMA prompts (all p values > .05), but they were younger (p = .031).
text.formatted: Excluded participants did not differ on gender, race, ethnicity, education level, or number of completed EMA prompts (all p values > .05), but they were younger (p = .031).

text.text: The 74 participants completed 2,773 prompts (M = 37.47 of 56), and 515 (18.6%) had no GPS fix within 15 minutes and were excluded, leaving 2,258 prompts for the athome models.
Hourly estimates were unavailable for a further 163 of these prompts (7.2%), so the time-spent-at-home models used 2,095 prompts for happiness (2,088 for anxiety and 2,093 for sadness).

The GPS data were collected through the Beiwe app using a burst-sampling approach: the GPS sensor was activated every 15 minutes for 90 consecutive seconds (on-cycle), during which location coordinates were recorded approximately every second when the device was in motion.

This approach was intended to minimize battery consumption while maintaining the ability to determine participant movement patterns and behavior throughout the day (Onnela et al., 2021; Straczkiewicz et al., 2021; Torous et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This approach was intended to minimize battery consumption while maintaining the ability to determine participant movement patterns and behavior throughout the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Onnela et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Straczkiewicz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Torous et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Participants reported their momentary emotional experiences at each prompt, including positive affect (Right now, how happy do you feel?
; between-person Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) = .36) and negative affect (Right now, how anxious do you feel?
; ICC = .43; Right now, how sad do you feel?
; ICC = .40), using a 4-point Likert scale from "Not at all" to "Very."

We used the Jasmine package (https://forest.beiwe.org/en/latest/jasmine.html) from the Forest Python library (Onnela et al., 2021; https://github.com/onnela-lab/forest) to impute missing data using a bidirectional sparse online Gaussian process approach and to characterize the resulting mobility trajectories from GPS data (Liu & Onnela, 2021).
text.formatted: We used the Jasmine package (<ref type="url" target="https://forest.beiwe.org/en/latest/jasmine.html">https://forest.beiwe.org/en/latest/jasmine.html</ref>) from the Forest Python library <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Onnela et al., 2021</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/onnela-lab/forest">https://github.com/onnela-lab/forest</ref>) to impute missing data using a bidirectional sparse online Gaussian process approach and to characterize the resulting mobility trajectories from GPS data <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Liu & Onnela, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we used the software package to compute hourly estimates of time spent at home based on inferred daily mobility trajectories.
We then calculated the time spent at home in minutes (range: 0-180) during the 3-hour period preceding each EMA prompt.
This window was selected to align with the EMA sampling design, in which participants reported on their current affect approximately every three hours.
This operationalization allows for the examination of how short-term cumulative time spent at home relates to momentary affect.
These analyses were not preregistered.

In addition, because Jasmine does not readily generate a binary indicator of whether participants were at home at the exact time of each EMA prompt, we implemented a data-driven clustering approach to estimate participants' home locations from raw, unprocessed GPS data.
Specifically, we used the density-based spatial clustering package DBSCAN to extract and cluster nighttime GPS observations (8 PM to 8 AM) within each participant's EMA study window.
The largest spatial cluster was defined as the participant's home location, and the home centroid was computed as the median latitude and longitude of this cluster.
We defined a participant-specific radius using the 95 th percentile of distances from cluster points to the centroid, capped at 200 meters to reduce the influence of GPS noise.
We then classified each EMA prompt as occurring at home versus outside the home based on the nearest GPS observation within a ±15-minute window and its distance from the home centroid.
The GPS-derived home indicator was validated against participants' self-reported location at each EMA prompt.
Agreement between the GPS-based classification and EMA selfreport was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and overall accuracy.
The GPS-based indicator demonstrated good agreement with self-report (sensitivity = 87.3%, specificity = 85.8%, PPV = 88.7%, NPV = 84.1%, accuracy = 86.7%).

Agreement was similar before any participant was excluded on the basis of GPS quality (accuracy = 84.9% across all 103 participants for whom a home location could be detected), indicating that the exclusions did not inflate the agreement estimate.
The high PPV indicates that when the GPS algorithm classified a participant as being at home, this classification was highly reliable.
A small number of participants for whom the algorithm consistently failed to detect home were excluded from analyses.

Exclusion required both a 100% false negative rate and a minimum of five EMA-reported home observations, a threshold chosen to parallel the minimum cluster density parameter (minPts = 5) used in the DBSCAN home detection algorithm, ensuring that exclusions reflected systematic algorithm failure rather than insufficient opportunity for home detection.

Time of day was categorized based on EMA sampling blocks (morning: 8 AM to 11:59 AM; midday: 12 PM to 3:59 PM; afternoon: 4 PM to 7:59 PM; evening: after 8 PM), and day of week was coded as weekday versus weekend.
These variables were included to examine temporal context and to test whether associations between time spent at home (at home versus outside) and affect varied across daily and weekly rhythms.
We used multilevel linear models with EMA prompts (Level 1) nested within individuals (Level 2).

Because prompts were also nested within study days, we examined a three-level null model (prompts within days within persons); the day-level intraclass correlation was modest (.14 for happiness, .18 for anxiety, and .19 for sadness).
We therefore retained the two-level specification for the primary analyses and re-estimated all substantive models with a three-level random-intercept structure (see Robustness Analyses below).
Separate models were fit for each affective outcome (happiness, anxiety, and sadness).
For models examining time spent at home, predictors were decomposed into within-person (WP) and between-person (BP) components.

The within-person component represented deviations from each participant's own mean level of time spent at home at a given prompt, whereas the between-person component represented each participant's average time spent at home across the study period.

Within-person predictors were person-mean centered, and between-person predictors were grand-mean centered, allowing us to distinguish momentary deviations from stable individual differences (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013).
text.formatted: Within-person predictors were person-mean centered, and between-person predictors were grand-mean centered, allowing us to distinguish momentary deviations from stable individual differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: First, we fit a temporal context model to examine whether time of day and day of week were independently associated with momentary affective outcomes (RQ1; Model 1).
Y ti reflects the momentary affect rating (happiness, anxiety, or sadness) reported by participant i at prompt t.
The superscripts WP and BP denote WP (person-mean-centered, indexed ti) and BP (grandmean-centered person mean, indexed i) components of these predictors.

Time of day was represented by three dummy-coded indicators, TimeOfDay K,ti (k = 1, 2, 3 for midday, afternoon, and evening, with morning as the reference category), so each time-of-day term in the equations denotes a set of three coefficients rather than a single coefficient.

DayOfWeek ti was coded 1 for Saturday and Sunday and 0 for weekdays. β 0i is the person-specific intercept, modeled at Level 2 as β 0i = γ 00 + u 0i , where γ 00 is the grand-mean intercept and u 0i ~ N(0, τ00) is the random intercept deviation of participant i.
The remaining β terms are fixed-effect coefficients, and e ti is the Level-1 residual.
In the primary models, Level-1 residuals were assumed independent, e ti ~ N(0, σ²):
Second and third, we estimated separate regression models to examine the effects of environmental context (home vs. outside) and time spent at home (RQ2 and RQ3) on momentary affect.

AtHome ti is a binary indicator of whether participant i was at home (1) or outside the home (0) at prompt t, and Home3h ti is the number of minutes (0 to 180) that participant i spent at home during the three hours preceding prompt t:

Fourth, we added the variables from Models 2 and 3 to the temporal base model (separately) to test whether environmental context or time spent at home improved model fit beyond temporal predictors, and to assess whether temporal and environmental contexts were jointly and independently associated with affective outcomes:
Finally, we conducted exploratory analyses to test moderation by temporal context (Models 5a and 5b).
These analyses tested whether WP association between home exposure and affect varied across temporal context.
Specifically, we included interaction terms between WP environmental context (home vs. outside) and time of day and day of week, as well as interactions involving time spent at home.

Because time of day contributes three interaction coefficients and weekend contributes one, the omnibus likelihood ratio test comparing each interaction model with its additive counterpart served as the primary test of temporal moderation; individual interaction coefficients are reported for completeness and interpreted only descriptively.
We compared models across steps using likelihood ratio tests, evaluating improvements in model fit with χ² difference tests and changes in AIC and BIC.

In a second set of exploratory analyses (Models 6a and 6b), we tested cross-level interactions between WP and BP components of each home-exposure indicator to examine whether the within-person association between home exposure and affect depended on how much time participants typically spent at home.
These models added the product of the WP and BP components to Models 4a and 4b, respectively:
Significant cross-level interactions were probed by estimating the simple slope of the WP effect at low (-1 SD), mean, and high (+1 SD) values of BP component.

Given the number of exploratory interaction tests (six omnibus temporal-moderation tests and six cross-level interaction tests across the three outcomes), we applied a Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction across these 12 tests.
Additionally, because random-intercept-only models can inflate Type I error rates for cross-level interactions (Heisig & Schaeffer, 2019), we treat these tests as exploratory.

Omnibus likelihood ratio tests, which jointly evaluated the three time-of-day interaction terms and the weekend interaction term, indicated that adding the interaction terms did not improve model fit over the additive models for either at home versus outside (happiness: χ²(4) = 3.41, p = .492; anxiety: χ²(4) = 2.17, p = .705; sadness: χ²(4) = 1.83, p = .767) or time spent at home (happiness: χ²(4) = 2.74, p = .602; anxiety: χ²(4) = 2.65, p = .618; sadness: χ²(4) = 1.45, p = .835).

text.text: Thus, the within-person associations between location (at home versus outside, or time spent at home) and affect did not vary by time of day or day of week.

Cross-level interactions (Models 6a and 6b) indicated that the within-person association between being at home (vs. outside the home) and affect did not vary as a function of how much time participants typically spent at home for any outcome (happiness: β = 0.205, SE = 0.236, p = .384; anxiety: β = 0.013, SE = 0.223, p = .955; sadness: β = 0.027, SE = 0.190, p = .887).
Likewise, the within-person association between recent time spent at home and anxiety or sadness did not depend on participants' average time spent at home (all p values > .05).

text.text: In the present study, we examined how temporal context, environmental context (at home versus outside), and recent exposure duration (time spent at home) related to momentary emotional experiences in young adults' daily lives.

Using a combination of EMA and passive GPS sensing data over 14 days, we found that spatial and temporal context were more consistently associated with variations in happiness than with negative affect in this young adult sample.

These findings extend digital phenotyping research by suggesting that GPS-derived environmental indicators relate to momentary emotional experience at the time when affect is assessed and that where and when people spend time are correlates of positive emotional experience in daily life.
The pattern of diurnal and weekly variation in affect was partly consistent with prior findings.
Participants reported greater happiness in the evening and at midday relative to morning, and on weekends relative to weekdays.
They also reported lower anxiety in the evening relative to the morning.
The evening peak in happiness is consistent with evidence of systematic diurnal variation in positive affect (Clark et al., 1989).
text.formatted: The evening peak in happiness is consistent with evidence of systematic diurnal variation in positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Clark et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: The direction of this variation, however, is inconsistent with that observed in large population-based samples, in which positive affect is highest in the morning and declines across the day (Bu et al., 2025; Golder & Macy, 2011).
text.formatted: The direction of this variation, however, is inconsistent with that observed in large population-based samples, in which positive affect is highest in the morning and declines across the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Golder & Macy, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For young adults in particular, whose mornings are often characterized by occupational and academic obligations across multiple life domains, along with fatigue following disrupted sleep (Adams et al., 2017; Dettmers et al., 2020; Kohler Giancola et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2024), the evening may represent a period of leisure and social engagement that promotes positive affect (e.g., less likely to work or attend classes in the evening).
text.formatted: For young adults in particular, whose mornings are often characterized by occupational and academic obligations across multiple life domains, along with fatigue following disrupted sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dettmers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kohler Giancola et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lu et al., 2024)</ref>, the evening may represent a period of leisure and social engagement that promotes positive affect (e.g., less likely to work or attend classes in the evening).

text.text: The weekend happiness effect is consistent with research linking days free of structured obligations with increased opportunity for social interaction and reduced academic and work stress (Adams et al., 2017; Ryan et al., 2010; Saleh et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The weekend happiness effect is consistent with research linking days free of structured obligations with increased opportunity for social interaction and reduced academic and work stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Ryan et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Saleh et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, anxiety did not differ between weekdays and weekends, which may reflect the stable nature of stress and obligation in young adulthood: occupational responsibilities, academic work, and interpersonal obligations do not fully recede on weekends for many young adults (Dettmers et al., 2020; Ryan et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In contrast, anxiety did not differ between weekdays and weekends, which may reflect the stable nature of stress and obligation in young adulthood: occupational responsibilities, academic work, and interpersonal obligations do not fully recede on weekends for many young adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dettmers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Ryan et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: It is also likely that distributional constraints limited sensitivity in this sample: most participants reported consistently low levels of anxiety (M = 1.64, SD = 0.85) and sadness (M = 1.41, SD = 0.71), with happiness (M = 2.72, SD = 0.86) falling closer to the scale midpoint and showing greater variability.
Participants also reported lower happiness when at home than when outside of the home at the within-person level.
Time outside the home provides greater opportunities for social interaction, which is associated with improved mood and reduced loneliness (Kuczynski et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Time outside the home provides greater opportunities for social interaction, which is associated with improved mood and reduced loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kuczynski et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For young adults whose social lives are often structured around academic/work and other obligations, being outside the home likely corresponds to greater engagement with peers and social environments.

Being outside also affords individuals greater access to varied and potentially restorative settings (e.g., natural environments and green spaces) that have been linked to replenishment of attentional resources and promotion of well-being (Houlden et al., 2018; Kangarloo et al., 2023; S. Kaplan, 1995).
text.formatted: Being outside also affords individuals greater access to varied and potentially restorative settings (e.g., natural environments and green spaces) that have been linked to replenishment of attentional resources and promotion of well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Houlden et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kangarloo et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">S. Kaplan, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The fact that this association persisted after accounting for temporal context suggests that environmental context was associated with happiness independently of when these exposures occurred.

Of note is that the GPS-based home classification, while validated against self-report with acceptable accuracy (overall accuracy = 86.7%), is an approximation; some EMA prompts may have been misclassified, and the precision of the ±15-minute GPS window may introduce noise, particularly during transition periods.
Additionally, being at home versus outside was not associated with anxiety or sadness.

One possibility is that the contextual factors examined here are insufficient to produce detectable within-person shifts in negative affect, which may require more psychologically potent triggers such as interpersonal conflict, academic failure, or illness.
Future work with samples showing greater affective variability would provide a stronger test of whether environmental context is associated with negative affect.

Within-person analysis results indicated that when individuals spent more time at home in the three hours preceding an EMA prompt (relative to their own typical level of home exposure), they reported lower happiness.

These associations are distinct from between-person differences: the absence of significant between-person effects for both at home versus outside and time spent at home indicates that individuals who habitually spent more time at home did not differ in average happiness from those who spent less.
Rather, it is the momentary deviation from one's own typical environmental exposure pattern, being at home more than usual on a given occasion, that is associated with lower happiness in that moment.
This within-person specificity suggests that the association cannot be attributed to stable between-person differences in lifestyle or routine.
However, this association does not rule out time-varying confounding or reverse directionality; for example, individuals may stay home more on occasions when they are already feeling less happy.

Unmeasured time-varying factors, including social engagement and sleep quality, may account for part of these associations, and future studies should consider multivariate passive sensing models that jointly model geolocation-derived indicators alongside social and activity data.

Additionally, the three-hour duration window was selected to align with the EMA sampling interval; shorter windows might capture more proximal associations while longer windows might better index sustained exposure patterns, and examining associations across multiple timescales would clarify the temporal grain at which home exposure is most strongly associated with affective experiences.

However, although the three-hour exposure window preceded each affect rating, affect during the exposure window itself was not assessed, so lower happiness may have preceded and contributed to remaining at home.

This caveat has particular relevance for the duration measure, which aggregates exposure over the preceding hours, whereas the concurrent at-home indicator captures location at the moment of assessment; neither measure supports causal inference.
Exploratory cross-level interactions tested whether these within-person associations varied as a function of participants' typical level of home exposure.
The within-person association between momentary home presence and affect generally did not depend on how much time participants typically spent at home.
In contrast, the within-person association between more time spent at home and lower happiness was stronger among individuals who typically spent less time at home.
Spending an unusually home-heavy few hours was associated with a larger reduction in happiness.
However, this cross-level interaction analysis was exploratory and was estimated without a random slope for the within-person term, so it should be treated as a hypothesis for future work.

If replicated, the pattern would be broadly consistent with evidence that day-to-day variety in the places people visit is associated with higher positive affect (Heller et al., 2020) and that being kept at home is harder on people who are usually out and about (Giuntella et al., 2021; Wijngaards et al., 2020).
text.formatted: If replicated, the pattern would be broadly consistent with evidence that day-to-day variety in the places people visit is associated with higher positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Heller et al., 2020)</ref> and that being kept at home is harder on people who are usually out and about <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giuntella et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wijngaards et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The cross-level interaction was not significant for anxiety or sadness, consistent with the absence of main effects for those outcomes.
In addition, happiness measured by a single item may not capture the full landscape of positive emotional experience, including distinctions in arousal (Russell, 1980).
text.formatted: In addition, happiness measured by a single item may not capture the full landscape of positive emotional experience, including distinctions in arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Russell, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Within the circumplex model of affect (Posner et al., 2005; Russell, 1980), positive states vary along both valence and arousal dimensions.
text.formatted: Within the circumplex model of affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Posner et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Russell, 1980)</ref>, positive states vary along both valence and arousal dimensions.

text.text: The contextual factors examined here may be more closely tied to higher-arousal positive experiences such as social excitement and engagement (McManus et al., 2024; Swerdlow et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The contextual factors examined here may be more closely tied to higher-arousal positive experiences such as social excitement and engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(McManus et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Swerdlow et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, home environments and extended time at home may support low-arousal positive states such as calmness and contentment that a single happiness item would not distinguish.

All associations with happiness reported here should therefore be interpreted as pertaining to the specific positive state captured by this item rather than to positive emotional experience broadly, and studies assessing affect across both valence and arousal dimensions are needed.
Exploratory analyses did not support a model whereby the association between location and affect varied as a function of time of day or day of week.
It is possible that with a larger sample, power to detect small interaction effects would be sufficient for moderation to emerge.
It is also possible that moderation would be more pronounced in populations for whom the psychological meaning of home time differs across temporal contexts.

For example, moderation might be more detectable among individuals with clearly demarcated work and leisure schedules, for whom being home on a weekday evening versus a weekend evening carries distinct implications for social opportunity and role obligation.
Alternatively, the absence of moderation may indicate that the association between home exposure and momentary happiness is relatively consistent across daily and weekly rhythms.

This study suggests that environmental contexts (i.e., at home versus outside and time spent at home) are associated with momentary happiness over and above temporal context in daily life, with young adults reporting lower happiness when at home and when they have spent more time at home in the preceding hours.

These associations were observed for happiness but not for anxiety or sadness and operated at the within-person level rather than between-person, a pattern consistent with, though not demonstrative of, dynamic context-affect coupling in real time.

The absence of associations with negative affect may point to differential contextsensitivity across the positive and negative dimensions of affect, although this possibility was not tested directly here.

Taken together, these findings suggest that where and when people spend time are associated with momentary positive emotional experience, and that integrating EMA with passive GPS sensing offers a productive path toward understanding how the spatial and temporal structure of daily life relates to emotional experiences.
